column11: Mishneh Torah, Human Dispositions 2:1: “In Mishneh Torah (Hilchot De’ot 2:1), Maimonides writes that just as a physician heals a patient whose body has drifted to one extreme by administering the opposite temperament until equilibrium is restored, so too one whose soul has become ill with a flawed character trait must incline toward the opposite extreme until he returns to the middle path.” Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 13, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Mishneh Torah, Human Dispositions 2:1) to illuminate his argument here (“in the manner that Maimonides wrote (Hilchot De'ot, chapter 2): that one who has fallen sick with the illness of bad character traits, his remedy is to seize the opposite extreme, and not the middle path; see there....”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.

column15: And within the soul of man this hints at holy deeds varying in their spiritual character: for there are virtuous actions that become permanently etched in the soul of man forever; and there are virtuous deeds of immense spiritual rarity whose holy energy disappears from man's conscious perception after their performance, as it is written (Psalms 95:4): “The peaks of the mountains are His”—meaning that the Blessed Name demonstrates that these deeds are supremely exalted.

column11: Sotah 17a: ‘§ Rabbi Akiva taught: If a man [ish] and woman [isha] merit reward through a faithful marriage, the Divine Presence rests between them. These two letters can be joined to form the name of God spelled yod, heh. But if due to licentiousness they do not merit reward, the Divine Presence departs, leaving in each word only the letters alef and shin, which spell esh, fire. Therefore, fire consumes them.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 17a) to illuminate his argument here (“(as written in Sotah 17a); mirroring the principle: no drop descends from Above unless two drops arise from below, and the two drops enter into him. column15: “The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits.” And my revered father explained in Mei HaShiloach: the dimensions of the Ark spell the word lashon : 30 (Lamed) cubits in height, 300 (Shin) in length, and 50 (Nun) in breadth; hinting that upon the tongue alone he was required to conceal his certainty and hide in the Ark, while in his inward heart he held steadfast trust in the Blessed Name.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 14:9: ‘It [man’s soul] is called by five names: nefesh (Genesis 2:7), ruaḥ (Ezekiel 37:14), neshama (Genesis 2:7), yeḥida (Psalms 22:21), ḥaya (Psalms 143:3). Nefesh – this refers to blood, as it is stated: “For blood is the soul [nefesh]” (Deuteronomy 12:23). Ruaḥ – because it ascends and descends, as it is stated: “Who knows the spirit of the sons of man? Does it ascend upward?” (Ecclesiastes 3:21). also means wind, which ascends and descends. Neshama – this refers to man’s intellect, as people say: Intellect is good. Ḥaya – because all of one’s limbs may die, but it [the soul] remains alive [ḥaya] in the body. Yeḥida – because all of one’s limbs are in pairs, but it [the soul] is solitary…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 13, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 14:9) to illuminate his argument here (“corresponding to the five Partzufim, which are the five well-known soul-levels (Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, Yechidah); and when man and woman arrive in the world mirroring the primordial Adam and Eve, who will...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And these five perfections mentioned there correspond to the five soul-levels recorded (Bereishit Rabbah 14:9), which are: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah; which are the five correspondences enumerated in Berakhot (10a) between the soul and the Blessed Name, wherein through the breath of life in his nostrils man equates to the power of the Father, as it were, and as will all be explained in its place at length.
column15: As in the Zohar (Lech Lecha 83a): When a man ascends to bed his soul departs, leaving in the body only an imprint of the spark of life; which remains perpetually awake, reviving the body's faculties in the morning. And so in the world at large a cosmic spark of life exists that never slept: King David (Sukkah 26b).

column15: And this is “Am I my brother's keeper?”—meaning: was it possible for me to withhold anger and nullify Your sovereign Will? And since the power of choice was removed from me, I am not culpable in this (see below, section 70). column11: Yoma 86b: ‘Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, as the penitent’s intentional sins are counted for him as unwitting transgressions, as it is stated: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity” (Hosea 14:2). The Gemara analyzes this: Doesn’t “iniquity” mean an intentional sin? Yet the prophet calls it stumbling, implying that one who repents is considered as though he only stumbled accidentally in his transgression. The Gemara asks: Is that so? Didn’t Reish Lakish himself say: Great is repentance, as one’s intentional sins are counted for him as merits, as it is stated: “And when the wicked turns from his wickedness, and does that which is lawful and right, he…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 15, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 86b) to illuminate his argument here (“in the spirit of "willful sins are transformed into merits" (Yoma 86b), and "in the place where penitents stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand" (Berakhot 34b), which is an even higher spiritual level,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And across all other transgressions this is so: through complete repentance from love, intentional sins are transformed into merits (zechuyos) and upon them he shall live (Yechezkel 18:21); meaning that after proper repentance and the presentation of the tribute-gift, he returns to be intimate and an inhabitant of the Palace as at the beginning with even greater strength, since the sins themselves ascend into the tally of mitzvos.
column15: And in Pe'ah (1:1): “Forgiving iniquity (nosei avon)”—an expression of intentional forgetting; for such is Hashem's rule: “If you forget your sin I remember, and if you remember I forget.” As in the Zohar (Vayikra 23b): When a man sins and casts it behind his back, the King commands: “Let his sin be made known to him,” extending judgment upon him; for he who is arrogant and forgets his sin, the Holy One steps forth to expose it so it not be forgotten.

column11: Berakhot 34b: ‘And the Gemara notes that this statement disagrees with the opinion of Rabbi Abbahu who holds that penitents are superior to the righteous. As Rabbi Abbahu said: In the place where penitents stand, even the full-fledged righteous do not stand, as it is stated: “Peace, peace upon him who is far and him who is near.” Peace and greeting is extended first to him who is far, the penitent, and only thereafter is peace extended to him who is near, the full-fledged righteous.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 15, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 34b) to illuminate his argument here (“and "in the place where penitents stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand" (Berakhot 34b), which is an even higher spiritual level, the level of "Walk before Me." And this is realized through wholeness,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And it is astonishing, for that is the very dispute in the chapter Ein Omedin [Berachos 34b]; and behold, there it is Rabbi Abbahu who stated that "in the place where penitents stand, etc." that a penitent is greater, and he himself authored the aggadah in Bereishis Rabbah cited above, see there! But in my opinion the plain explanation is the reverse: Rabbi Abbahu is entirely consistent with his view that a penitent is greater, and for this reason he framed it, "I do not know in which He delights": for according to the one who holds a wholly righteous person is greater, it is obvious that He delights more in the deeds of the righteous.
column15: Meaning, each person holds an ordered book engraved in his heart from the providential circumstances Hashem leads him through, seeing He is the Cause of all causes; yet striving in concrete action cannot be taken gratis, but only through full payment; for active mitzvot embody deep Torah wisdom beyond human intellect, which Hashem enclothed within physical actions.

column11: Shemot Rabbah 36:2: ‘It is not that I need them, but rather, it is so that you illuminate for Me just as I illuminated for you. Why? It is to elevate you before all the nations, so that they will say: ‘Israel illuminates for the One who illuminates for all.’ This is analogous to a sighted person and a blind person who were walking. The sighted person said to the blind person: ‘Come and I will guide you,’ and the blind person was walking. When they entered the house, the sighted person said to the blind person: ‘Go kindle the lamp for me, and illuminate for me, so you will not be beholden to me for accompanying you. That is why I am telling you to illuminate.’ So, the sighted person is the Holy One blessed be…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 15, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shemot Rabbah 36:2) to illuminate his argument here (“And this is the secret of the lamps in the Temple, concerning which our Sages expounded (Shemot Rabbah 36:2): on the verse "You yearn for the work of Your hands" (Job 14:15): the Holy One illuminates all, etc.; for...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.

column15: And likewise what is stated: “You do not revere the Sanctuary, but Him who commanded concerning the Sanctuary”—showing that between Hashem and the Temple an intermediary also stands. And this explains the Midrash: Had it said “God created heaven and earth,” we would have thought they were deities—meaning we would have assumed heaven and earth themselves were the ultimate essential Will.

column11: Job 14:15: ‘You would call and I would answer You;You would set Your heart on Your handiwork.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 15, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Job 14:15) to illuminate his argument here (“on the verse "You yearn for the work of Your hands" (Job 14:15): the Holy One illuminates all, etc.; for although we know that He illuminates the entire world, we kindle light before Him because He so commanded.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: However, one who truly needs it derives genuine nourishment from it, but the Blessed Name has no need for it; so you must not say "I am doing His will, etc." as with all other commandments, but rather "to your desire"—in accordance with your own inner will and longing, so is the quality of the sacrifice. The only gratification to the Blessed Name arises directly from this: from their heartfelt desire and longing to please Him.
column15: “You will call”—this means that the Blessed Name initiates the call to man; and what is this call? The Blessed Name implants longing and yearning within the human heart. Afterward, man expresses and actualizes that call outwardly, so that it fulfills “You will yearn for the work of Your hands”—meaning that it may be credited as the handiwork of man.

column11: Sifrei Bamidbar 143: ‘(Bamidbar 28:8) "And the second lamb": Why is this written? Since it is written "the one lamb shall you offer in the morning," I might think that if it were not offered in the morning it could be offered in the evening. It is, therefore, written "the second shall you offer up towards evening," implying that if the morning tamid had not been offered, the evening tamid is not to be offered. When is this so? When the altar had not been inaugurated. But if it had been inaugurated, even the first may be offered in the evening. R. Shimon said: When is this so? When they were unwitting or under constraint (in not offering it in the morning), but if they were deliberate (in not doing so), if…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 15, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Sifrei Bamidbar 143) to illuminate his argument here (“and it is a gratification before Him that He spoke and His will was done (Sifrei Pinchas 143), behold, this itself is considered casting illumination before Him, as it were, in that Israel observe His pure...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And according to his words, over these three the fire of Gehinnom would have held dominion to consume completely, implying even if he were a Torah scholar, since he spoke generally of all who descend; and one must force according to his words that what was stated regarding Jewish sinners and scholars that fire cannot dominate excludes these three; but according to his words one can say that it refers to all who actually descend, excluding those who do not descend.
column15: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” The inner meaning of this is that the primordial light was overwhelmingly immense, to the extent that created beings were entirely unable to receive it; therefore the Blessed Name constricted this light so that it might become accessible within human comprehension.

column11: Shabbat 88a: ‘Rabbi Simai taught: When Israel accorded precedence to the declaration “We will do” over the declaration “We will hear,” 600,000 ministering angels came and tied two crowns to each and every member of the Jewish people, one corresponding to “We will do” and one corresponding to “We will hear.” And when the people sinned with the Golden Calf, 1,200,000 angels of destruction descended and removed them from the people, as it is stated in the wake of the sin of the Golden Calf: “And the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Horeb onward” (Exodus 33:6). column13: And in any event, according to a certain spiritual plane of that Sage worms had no dominion, unlike the plane of the other, each operating within its level; and so too here: if he did not effect completely to be under Rabbi himself, he became a footstool beneath some soul-spark of his, as is known that every soul branches into numerous sparks across generations, having minute branches that yet stem from the same root as the heel to the brain, but a prayer that achieved nothing at all would presumably never have been recorded in the Talmud].
column15: Yet after the Flood “the Lord said unto His heart”—unto the unique tzaddikim of each generation: “I will not again...” — charging them never again to separate themselves from their contemporaries, but to surrender their lives for the preservation of the collective totality; and once this vital heart-point refuses to separate, no universal destruction can ever strike the collective again.

column13: This is through Yehudah. But the “drawing of a teaching to its halachic conclusion” in this world — for the “walking” of people — [relates to] “when you walk [by the way]” — which is the toil of this world — and as the Sages said (Sotah 21a) on the verse “when you walk about, it shall lead you” (Mishlei 6:22), [referring] to the “walking” of this world; and this is the term “halachah,” which is “the conduct of walking” — [and] it is in Levi and Yissachar.
column15: Rather, the Sabbath of this physical world is not the bare Essence of divine Will, but contains vitality and radiance from Hashem through an intermediary, and that inner radiance is the true objective. Thus saving a life sets aside only the external garment of the commandment, not the essential divine Will, for the essential Will never changes; and within preserving a life is enfolded that very essential Will found within Shabbat, since preserving a Jewish soul preserves the Sabbath itself.

column11: Bava Metzia 86a: ‘The attendants said to Rabba bar Naḥmani: What should we do with him? He is the king’s man, and we cannot leave him like this. Rabba bar Naḥmani said to them: Place a tray before him and give him one cup to drink, and then remove the tray from before him and he will be healed. They did this, and he was healed. The messenger said: I am certain that the man I seek is here, as this unnatural event must have befallen me on his account. He searched for Rabba bar Naḥmani and found out where he was. The messenger said that they should tell Rabba bar Naḥmani: I will leave this inn and will not disclose your location. Even if they will kill that man, i.e., me, I will not disclose your location.…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 15, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 86a) to illuminate his argument here (“and in chapter HaPoalim (there, 86a): "let Rabbah bar Nachmani decide," and likewise this principle regarding the sanctification of the New Moon: "I and you shall go to the earthly court, to see when they have...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: And Ravina, who represented the end of halachic instruction in Babylonia and was among the sealers of the Talmud and the Oral Torah (Bava Metzia 86a), attained a trace and root in this as well; and he stated there: "I will debate and purify it by an a fortiori argument from the serpent, etc." (Eruvin 13b);] at Yavneh who would purify the sheretz with a hundred and fifty reasons. Ravina said: I will debate and purify it — and if a snake, which kills and increases impurity, is [itself] pure, a sheretz, which does not kill and increase impurity, all the more so [should be pure]!
